speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while ordinarily no reference is made in the House of Commons to those who in the past have been associated with the house, I trust that I may be permitted to make reference to the passing of one who had a signal honour conferred upon him on September 15, 1949 by a motion of the then prime minister, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. I refer, of course to Dr. Arthur Beauchesne. At that time he retired as Clerk of the House of Commons and had conferred upon him an appointment as honorary officer of the house and a seat at the table on occasions of ceremony.
Dr. Beauchesne passed away today in his eighty-third year. He made his mark in life as clerk assistant, to which post he was appointed in 1916, and as clerk of the house from 1925 to 1949. Those of us who were in the House of Commons during the days when he served as clerk of this house recognized him as a great scholar, a student and authority on parliamentary procedure. In his person, and through the instrumentality of his book on the rules of procedure in parliament he gave to parliament a singular distinction. I know that members on all sides of the house would want to pay their tribute to this honorary officer of the House of Commons who, though he retired some 10 years ago, retained a position by virtue of the motion to which I referred. This was not the first time in Canada's history, I believe, but the second occasion upon which an outstanding clerk had been so honoured. I wish to extend the sympathy of the House of Commons to the family of Dr. Beauchesne.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is
entirely appropriate that the Prime Minister should have expressed, on behalf of the house, our very great regret and sorrow at the news of Dr. Beauchesne's passing. Dr. Beauchesne, of course, has made a great and permanent contribution to parliamentary government and parliamentary institutions in Canada. He has become over the years as the Prime Minister has indicated, the acknowledged master of parliamentary procedure,
and his published works on this subject have become, of course, a bible for us all. As long as we are preoccupied in this house with points of order, rules and procedure, and that will be as long as there is parliamentary government in Canada, Dr. Beauchesne's name will perhaps appear in the columns of Hansard more often than that of any member.
His public service to Canada in this and in other capacities extended over many years, indeed until the very last days of his life. I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that service will not be forgotten by the country which has benefited so greatly from his work. We on this side of the house should like to join with the Prime Minister in this expression of regret and sympathy to the surviving members of Dr. Beauchesne's family.

Mr. Speaker, we in the C.C.F. group wish to be associated with the expression of sympathy of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition. It was my good fortune to serve in the House of Commons from 1945 to 1949 while Dr. Beauchesne was still the clerk. All of us who knew him personally recognized his great knowledge of parliamentary procedure. I think it was fitting that he was interested in parliamentary procedure almost to his very last breath. The fourth edition of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms was published only last year. Dr. Beauchesne has a permanent place in the life of parliamentary government, having served Canada so well and having established himself as Canada's eminent authority on parliamentary rules and forms.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members are aware, Canada was represented at the NATO ministerial meeting by the Minister of National Defence who will not be returning to Ottawa until tomorrow, and who no doubt will add to some general observations that I make on this occasion in answer to the Leader of the Opposition in giving to the house a brief account of the position taken by Canada on the principal questions discussed at the meeting.
As a result of the Soviet union's declared intentions concerning Berlin and Germany, the discussions of the council were largely devoted to the consideration of the German problem in its various aspects. The ministerial council received a report from the four powers with special responsibilities for the German question, on the present state of their thinking in respect to those matters which will be the subject of discussion during the forthcoming talks with the Soviet union.
The Berlin issue is undoubtedly one of the most serious challenges that the alliance has yet had to face. Canada considers it imperative that it should not be interpreted primarily as a challenge to our military capability, as a challenge to seek a solution by force. We believe with President Eisenhower, in the words he used some years ago, "there is no alternative to peace". Believing that, the west must therefore try to settle its differences with the Soviet union by negotiation. But if these negotiations are to be successful there is a clear need to clarify western thinking with respect to the grave issues confronting the alliance. This was one of the purposes of the meeting in Washington.
By way of contributing to this process of clarification Canada offered a few suggestions concerning the problem of Berlin. In the Canadian view no agreement can be acceptable to the west which places in jeopardy the security of West Berlin or the freedom of its citizens. It is also the Canadian view that the NATO countries could not accept a solution which might endanger the ties between the Federal Republic of Germany and the other countries of western Europe. Moreover, we could not accept arrangements which might have the effect of foreclosing the prospect of the reunification of Germany.
Hon. members will recall that I made a statement in this house on March 19 in which I expressed the belief that-
-the United Nations might play some significant role in the solution of the Berlin problem, and that this phase deserves further and more careful study.
In the development of this idea the Canadian delegation suggested that the permanent council of NATO study the possibility

of a role for the United Nations in the application of a solution for the Berlin problem. I believe the United Nations might play a useful role provided, of course, that a four-power agreement is reached first. The basic role of the United Nations might be to verify that all parties were abiding by the terms of the agreement. An essential part of the agreement might be a Soviet pledge binding itself and its associates to full freedom of access to West Berlin and the acceptance of a "United Nations presence" on the lines of communication to that city. Canada, in advancing these suggestions as a basis for discussion, emphasized that United Nations responsibility for West Berlin would be complementary to the rights and obligations of the four occupying powers.
With regard to the problem of a German settlement, the Canadian delegation expressed the hope that there would be increasing cooperation at the technical level between the federal republic and the East German regime. It would, in the Canadian view, be fruitful to give further study to a proposal originally made by the federal German republic to institute a continuing commission for Germany which would be charged with the responsibility for supervising and promoting progress toward reunification. The Canadian delegation further suggested that the western powers might usefully explore the possibility of some measure of arms limitation which, together with an adequate system of inspection and control, might have a wholesome and calming effect in the European area.
I think we can say with some satisfaction that the four members of the alliance with special responsibility in Berlin not only received with careful attention the suggestion made by the Canadian delegation and other members of the council, but they have agreed to take into account in their preparatory work the views and observations put forward during the ministerial meeting for the difficult negotiations which lie ahead. I submit this is another important development in effective political consultation in NATO matters which will be of great importance to each and to all members of the alliance.
If there are further matters that the minister of defence can bring before the house amplifying what I have stated today, the opportunity will come upon his return to the house.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the Minister of National Defence, as the Prime Minister has said, will be making perhaps a more detailed statement on an appropriate occasion on his return to the house, I need not comment at any length on what the Prime Minister has just said; but I think

the house will welcome his statement, especially as the NATO communique from Washington was not very comprehensive or informative in regard to the questions which are very much in our minds, particularly the question of Germany and Berlin.
There is no doubt, as the Prime Minister has said, that the west is entitled, and indeed has a duty, to display firmness in regard to the protection of western rights in Berlin, though firmness itself is not necessarily a policy so much as a posture. There are western rights in Berlin which have to be protected, but there are also eastern interests in Berlin and, indeed, in Germany; and the problem is, of course, to reconcile western rights with eastern interests. I think we in this house all agree that this must be done by negotiation and cannot be done by force. It has therefore become a matter for negotiation.
So far as we on this side of the house are concerned, we support the principles which the Prime Minister has in a general and brief way indicated as the basis for such negotiations. We think the Canadian proposal put forward at the NATO council for the introduction of the United Nations into this Berlin situation in some appropriate way was a constructive and imaginative one. We hope this proposal can be followed up by the NATO council.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON WASHINGTON
speechtext:
We welcome the stand taken by the Canadian government in advancing the possibility of the United Nations playing a useful role in the Berlin crisis. Nothing the west does should imperil either the security or the freedom of the people of West Berlin, but there is a growing feeling, I believe, in the NATO nations that this is a time for negotiation, a time for discussion. Perhaps, working with the United Nations, agreement might be reached which would maintain the security and the freedom of West Berlin while at the same time showing the Soviet union that the western world is prepared to take into consideration its natural fear of a rearmed and reunited Germany.
It is no secret that there are great strains at this time within the NATO organization. We hope that cool heads will prevail. We hope that the stand taken by the Canadian government, the position outlined by the Prime Minister and the position taken by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, will prevail to the end that negotiation and settlement may be achieved. We are hopeful that a summit meeting will take place, and that at that time a lasting solution to this problem will be reached.

20. Landing in Canada of any person is prohibited except where the person falls within one of the following classes of persons who may be landed in Canada if such person meets the requirements of the act and of these regulations:
(a)	a person who is a British subject by birth or by naturalization in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, or the Union of South Africa, a citizen of Ireland, a citizen of France born or naturalized in France or in St. Pierre and Miquelon islands, or a citizen of the United States of America if such person has sufficient means to maintain himself in Canada until he has secured employment therein;
(b)	a person who is a citizen by birth or by naturalization of Austria, Belgium, Denmark, the Federal Republic of Germany, Finland, Greece, Iceland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden or Switzerland or who is a refugee from a country of Europe, if such person undertakes to come to Canada for placement under the auspices of the department or, if the department has given its approval thereto, for establishment in a business, trade or profession or in agriculture;
(c)	a person who is a citizen by birth or by naturalization of Egypt, Israel, Lebanon, Turkey, or of any country of Europe or of a country of North America, Central America or South America if such person is the husband, wife, son, daughter, brother, sister, as well as the husband or wife and the unmarried children under 21 years of age of any such son, daughter, brother or sister, as the case may be-
And so forth.
Subsection (c) was amended in only two particulars, one by deleting Egypt as one of the countries, and by altering son and daughter to unmarried son and daughter, and

The hon. member has raised a question about our practice, and I think perhaps I should make a preliminary comment on it. I have had some concern about the practice which has grown up of making rather lengthy statements in reply to questions rather than making such statements under the heading of motions, which has been the customary practice.
Today we have had two examples. The Leader of the Opposition asked a question, in reply to which the Prime Minister made a rather extensive statement on a matter of public interest which could have been made as a statement under the heading of motions. Then in response to a question from the hon. member for Davenport we have had another answer which is perhaps more in the nature of a statement, in that it deals with a matter


at greater length than has been the practice in answering questions. There is perhaps confusion as between the two procedures which are available at this stage of the proceedings of the house; first, statements by ministers followed by comment by one speaker from the official opposition and one from the other group and, second, the usual oral question and answer practice.
Without giving any settled opinion or ruling I do say this is a problem the house must bear in mind, because it becomes confusing if we do not keep separate the procedure respecting ministerial statements and comment thereon and the procedure as to oral questions and answers.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF PROJECT AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. I also have a question from the hon. member for St. John's East which I shall answer at the same time, and which reads as follows:
Would the minister comment on the accuracy of a statement made in the Newfoundland legislature, Friday, April 3, by Premier Smallwood, and as reported by the Canadian Press, to the effect "that C.M.H.C. had taken from the St. John's housing authority the possession and administration of 192 rental units, contrary to a 1956 agreement"?
The general practice in setting up authorities to administer dominion-provincial housing projects is for representatives of the two governments, that is federal and provincial and in most cases also the municipal authority concerned, to agree upon the personnel to be appointed to the authority in question. Appointments are then made by provincial order

in council. This plan has been followed successfully in the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba, British Columbia and Saskatchewan, and there has been the closest co-operation among the three levels of government. In the provinces of Alberta and Prince Edward Island there are no dominion-provincial housing projects.
This course was not followed in Newfoundland, where a St. John's housing authority was set up by the provincial government in 1951. The administration of dominion-provincial projects by this authority eventually proved to be unsatisfactory, and early in 1958 it was understood that inactive members would be removed and that new appointments would be made pursuant to consultation between representatives of the two governments. However, the provincial government failed to carry out such consultations and filled the authority with its own appointees, in spite of the fact that 75 per cent of the cost of these projects, including the cost of rental subsidies, is paid from the federal treasury.
On August 25, 1958 I wrote to Premier Smallwood-I shall table these letters-suggesting a method of co-operating in the administration of the housing projects in St. John's, but have received no reply. I wrote again on October 2, 1958. No reply having been received from the premier to either of these letters, I wrote again on February 10, 1959, as there were two new dominion-provincial housing projects nearing completion, but as yet no reply to the third letter has been received.
In the light of these circumstances Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which has been building these two further projects, is administering any units in the two new projects which are available for occupation, and tenants are being chosen entirely on the basis of need, which I am afraid was not the case when the provincial government was administering them. I am hopeful that it will be possible to work out a satisfactory method of co-operation between the two governments, just as has been done in the other provinces.
May I add that press reports indicate that we have been accused of playing politics in the allotment of housing for poor people, but all the evidence I have been able to get is to the effect that the shoe is on the other foot. Hitherto, in some cases, people have had to apply to the provincial government in order to get accommodation. I should like to table these three letters.

speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, not this one. The hon. member gave me notice of this question, for which I thank him. His information was drawn, I believe, from the Coarse Grain Quarterly published in February by the dominion bureau of statistics, and his

figures are in accordance with that document. On the face of it the picture looks gloomy, but there is a bright silver lining if you read a little further in the booklet, something which my hon. friend did not do.
The coarse grains are divided chiefly into barley and oats. The barley export, which normally runs at about 75 million bushels in a crop year, I think will be attained this year. Our barley exports are a little above what they were a year ago. The barley goes to the United Kingdom in large part and to the United States, Germany and Japan. If you separate the barley from the oats, it is the oats that give the poorer picture because the exports there are down a bit; and that is largely because the export market for oats, running to about 20 million bushels a year, has been largely the United States, and the supply of feed in the United States is 12 per cent greater than it was a year ago. Of course when you put the two together you get an average which gives a poorer picture than is actually the case, because our substantial barley exports will be maintained and the oats picture may be improved.

Does this mean that if a further increase in wages takes place and is reflected in a second increase in freight rates, the government would follow the same pattern and increase the $20 million subsidy to meet the position brought about by the further increase in the rates?
That is a hypothetical question and one which I should not care to answer now.

Mr. Chairman, I want to add my words to what has been said by the previous speaker. With all due deference to the minister there are a number of things that are not clear even in the wording of the resolution itself or the purport as given to the committee in the statement made by the minister just prior to the Easter recess. I believe the committee has the right, in view of the importance of this matter, to ask the minister for a lucid explanation and exposition before the bill goes to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
One point the minister has made clear is that this represents only a temporary alleviation of the freight rate situation. The minister is asking for authority to pay up to an aggregate amount of $20 million in order to reduce the effect of the freight rate increase of recent date by some 7 per cent. But this entire question goes much deeper than that. I sincerely hope that while we are at the resolution stage the minister will take us more fully into his confidence.
This afternoon on orders of the day I endeavoured to ask a question, and I wish now to repeat it in view of the statement made by the Speaker of this house. The question I asked was as follows:
It is our understanding that a royal commission is to be appointed to investigate the entire situation relative to freight rates. Can the Prime Minister inform the house whether or not in the terms of reference there will be authority to study a national transportation policy and make recommendations with respect thereto?
When I asked that question on the orders of the day the Speaker immediately rose and with the endorsation of the Prime Minister said that I was asking a question dealing with a matter of business that would come before us this afternoon. I am sure all hon. members would be interested in having the minister answer this question. We would like to know what he and the government have in mind with respect to transportation and freight rates, not just for the next 12 months under temporary alleviation in the form of subsidies but in the long term view.
If we can accept what we have heard on the radio and seen in the newspapers it is the intention of the government to appoint a royal commission. Surely it is the responsibility of the minister at this time, when
[Mr. Hees.l
he is asking for a subsidy of $20 million, to tell us what the government has in mind when the 12 month period is over. What has it in mind about the appointment of a royal commission? What personnel will serve on the royal commission? Perhaps of even greater importance, what will be the terms of reference of that commission? Surely this is the time, at the resolution stage of this legislation, when this information should be given to the committee. We sincerely hope the minister and the government do not have in mind simply allowing this matter to drift from year to year in the future as it has in the past.
If the government has in mind the appointment of a royal commission, what will be the terms of reference? Will it deal only with the question of freight rates? Does the government intend to follow a policy of allowing this question to drift from year to year, bringing in temporary measures in the form of subsidies? What we should have now and indeed what we should have had years ago is a thorough study into the transportation system in Canada, out of which would flow recommendations concerning a national transportation policy.
The time is long past when this country should have had a national transportation policy. Naturally there are great difficulties relating to this question. We have in Canada two great transportation systems, one publicly and one privately owned. Irrespective of this we must recognize that Canada is a large country, 3,500 miles in breadth, with a greater land area than the United States and a population of only 17,300,000, according to the latest figures. We require an efficient transportation system. I presume the intention of the royal commission would be to make recommendations in this regard, but as yet we have heard nothing from the minister with respect to this matter. We urge the minister to give us some information on this question this afternoon. We are interested in knowing the terms of reference of any royal commission that may be appointed. In particular we wish to be advised if one of those terms of reference will be a complete study of a national transportation system and recommendations for a national transportation policy. There is certainly a need for it.
I remember that years ago I had the privilege of being a member of the British Columbia legislature, at which time I met a most extraordinary individual. I did not like his politics nor did I like him personally, but I hasten to admit that he was a most unusual man. His name was G. G. McGeer. He was mayor of the city of Vancouver at one time, a member of the

British Columbia legislature, and a member of the House of Commons and the Senate. His was a rather outstanding experience. He was also one of the most outstanding lawyers in the province of British Columbia. Years ago a Liberal government appointed him as its counsel in a hassle on freight rates. I can still recall G. G. McGeer telling me with a chuckle how in five minutes he had won the case for British Columbia by producing a relief map that showed that in the main the territory from Calgary to Vancouver was downhill.
British Columbia won its case immediately but it has not won another case since or none of any importance so far as the transportation system and freight rates are concerned. Anyone who knows our country and particularly the western provinces can see the need for a national transportation policy. If you are a tourist travelling by train there is no question whatsoever but that you should travel on the C.P.R. through the Canadian Rockies and British Columbia's four mountain ranges. The trip is wonderful and the scenery is beautiful but the route is a very expensive one as far as the C.P.R. is concerned.
Yet about 200 miles north you have the C.N.R. line with practically no grades whatsoever. There is the route of freight whereas the C.P.R. line is the route of passengers. However, there has never been any co-ordination or correlation so far as passenger and freight traffic are concerned. Apparently the C.P.R. can set freight rates indirectly one way or another on the basis of their high cost route through the mountains of British Columbia instead of freight rates being set on the basis of the low cost route of the C.N.R.
It would be very interesting if the minister would tell us how fast a train can travel from Vancouver to Montreal. There is no difference in travel time between Vancouver and Montreal in the case of the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. even though the C.N.R. can undoubtedly make the trip in less time. All you have to do is to talk to the engineers, superintendents and firemen. There is no question at all that the C.N.R. could provide a faster trip but for some reason or other it is not allowed to do so. I do not know what the reasons are, but surely there is firm foundation for a real study to be made of a national transportation policy that will give the greatest efficiency at the lowest possible cost in the movement of both passengers and freight.
The fact that this afternoon the minister is asking the house for authority to subsidize both railways, one publicly owned and the other privately owned, to the extent of $20 million in one year provides ample reason for members of the house and taxpayers generally who have to pay the $20 million to ask
Freight Rates
the Minister of Transport to give the house this afternoon a clearer indication and a better understanding of what he has in mind from a long range point of view, what he intends to do to take care of the situation when the year is over and the $20 million is expended.
We understand, as I said before, that there is going to be a royal commission. We hope the minister will tell us who are going to be on the commission. If he cannot do that, at least he must know now what the terms of reference are. We ask the minister to take us into his confidence, to give us a picture of the terms of reference which will reveal the extent of the study and what authority is going to be given to the commission. We ask the minister to explain, if he does nothing else, whether or not under his direction as Minister of Transport there is going to be in the not too distant future a national transportation policy for the Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to make a few comments on the resolution and the whole principle involved in the subsidizing of railroads. Generally speaking I cannot say I am very favourable to the principle of subsidizing railroads because for one reason I do not think it is any solution at all to the freight rate problem. However, I believe it is justified in this case because it is going to help those parts of the country which suffer from discrimination in freight rates and I hope that the royal commission to be established will come up with a more permanent solution.
One thing that has surprised me is that in the course of the debate there has been no mention of what impact the subsidizing of railroads will have on other forms of transport. Surely one of the things that has kept freight rates down throughout the country is other forms of transport, water transport and truck transport. So far as the principle of subsidizing railroads is concerned, I think it would be very dangerous as a long term policy and I was pleased to hear the minister say that this provision is definitely only for one year and that a royal commission is to be appointed to consider the whole question.
There are some things that it will be hard for a royal commission to deal with; in fact, I do not see how a royal commission can deal with them under the terms of reference of the last royal commission. There has been some suggestion that if we have a thorough investigation it will solve the problem forever but no previous royal commission has ever solved it forever and if we have a commission now I do not expect it will solve it forever. However, the commission will probably be

Freight Rates
able to make suggestions that will help the situation for a few years. Because the situation changes from time to time I do not think we can expect a permanent solution, no matter what study we undertake now, that will solve the problem forever.
One of the things a royal commission is up against in investigating the whole matter is the difficulty of investigating the trucking industry. I am going to deal with the trucking industry particularly because I happen to know something about it. It is one of the main competing forms of transport so far as the railroads are concerned, and perhaps the real solution to freight rate discrimination would be to have more competition by truck transport in those areas where it is deficient at the present time. Obviously rates have been brought down in those areas where there is considerable truck transport and I do not see why rates would not be brought down if truck competition were expanded in those areas where there is discrimination. It seems to me that would be the logical way to achieve equalization of freight rates.
If we were to adopt a long term policy of subsidizing the railroads in those areas where there is discrimination surely the only thing we would do would be to prevent any competition arising because such subsidization would make it impossible for truck competition to develop. If we were to adopt such a long term policy we would be spending money in this manner which I think could be much better spent to promote the building of highways with the object of bringing down freight rates in that way.
I should like to deal for a moment with two or three aspects of the trucking industry. The last royal commission, the Turgeon commission, was very much aware of the impact of trucking on railways. However, under its terms of reference that commission was unable to go too far in investigating the trucking industry because it did not come within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. You will recall that the Turgeon report was made before the privy council decided that certain aspects of the trucking industry did in fact come within the scope of the federal parliament.
I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members the various groups that are engaged in the trucking industry and what their effect has been on rail rates. We first of all have the group known as for-hire operators who perform exactly the same service as the railroads do. They maintain their trucks for hire by the general public and they charge a fee for moving freight. The second group involved in truck transport is the private owners. This is a group of businessmen who maintain trucks for the purpose

of moving their own goods from place to place. I do not think any real assessment has been made up to the present time of their impact on the field of transportation because nobody on the federal level has had the authority to investigate this question. Since the last royal commission was set up to inquire into freight rates there has been one new segment added to the trucking industry and that is the U-drive trucks. These trucks are leased and a man can hire the truck for a day, a week or a month, to move his own goods.
Now, each one of these segments of the trucking industry has an effect on freight rates. The main point is that there is some regulation, in fact there is a growing body of regulation over the for-hire truckers. However, there is practically no regulation of the private operators, nor do I believe that they pay a fair share of the taxes. I am not familiar with the situation across Canada, but I can speak for the province of British Columbia.
I cannot quote figures which are up to date because the situation has been changed. A department of transport has been set up under the provincial government and some radical changes have been made in the taxation structure. The field of taxation with relation to trucking is quite broad, but one aspect of it is the highway licence which is required. A few years ago I recall that this licence cost in the neighbourhood of $180 for a truck operated by a for-hire operator, whereas the operator using his own truck paid somewhere in the neighbourhood of $5. There are many other fields in which I believe this tax discrimination exists. I feel that it has a great effect on freight rates because these people who operate their own trucks tend to keep down the rates of the for-hire operator. Shippers tend to say to the for-hire operators, "If you do not keep your rates down, we will buy our own trucks." This, in turn, has caused the railroads to set up what they call competitive rates across Canada.
It is my contention that these competitive rates are, in many instances, too low. I believe this has resulted in added freight rate discrimination because obviously the railroads have to be aware of their total revenue situation. If they cannot get revenue in one place, obviously they have to apply higher rates wherever the traffic will bear them. I think this fact is to a great extent responsible for the discrimination that exists in freight rates today. I do not see how any investigation by a royal commission that does not have authority to deal with all the aspects of trucking, and to determine whether trucks are paying their proper share of taxation for

the use of the roads, and various other questions of this nature, can ever arrive at any proper settlement of this freight rate question. I do not think we should even consider investigating the railroad industry by iself, without taking into consideration the trucking industry, water transport and air transport which I am sure as time goes on is going to become more and more important.
I know that somebody is going to tell me we will not have authority to do this because trucking comes within the jurisdiction of the provinces. However, I want to say this: most of the people who come here to make complaints about freight rates have been the provincial governments. I certainly feel that under the circumstances, when the provincial governments have such a great interest in this matter, there could be more co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. We seem to arrive at this same situation in so many fields of legislation today. When we come to deal with some subject we find that part of it comes under the federal government and part of it comes under the provincial government. I believe that the question of freight rates is one subject where the interests of these governments are common. It may be that whatever type of commission is set up, eventually provincial representatives of some sort could be appointed. In any case, I certainly believe that any investigation must take into consideration the impact of the trucking industry on this whole question of freight rates.
There are one or two other things that I believe the federal government could do which would help the situation. At the moment there are no provisions under the Railway Act for the trucking industry to appear before the board of transport commissioners when freight rate hearings are held. I believe that the trucking industry has now reached a stage in which it could provide valuable information to the board of transport commissioners in making decisions. It may well be that the discrimination in existing freight rates comes about because they are too low in certain areas and, consequently, have to be raised too high in others. We have the railroads setting competitive rates. They say the rates are there to meet the competition of trucks or to meet the competition of water carriers. The water carriers are able to appear before the board of transport commissioners and state their views as to whether or not there is a competitive rate. In so far as the trucking industry is concerned, they are not allowed to appear before the board of transport commissioners to state their views on this matter.
It may well be that the competitive rates of the railroads in those areas where they 66968-9-146
Freight Rates
are meeting truck competition are lower than they need to be to meet this truck competition. I should like to cite one example of this which has come to my attention in British Columbia. I do not know to what extent this situation exists across Canada, but here is one instance in which the competitive rates of the railroads have been below the existing truck rates. It seems obvious to me that if the railroads lower freight rates in one place like that, then they have to raise them higher in another area in order to keep up their total revenue position. I do not think we can accept the fact that just because the public is making a saving in one particular area it is for the general good to have the railroads do that.
There are only two results which can flow from this practice. When the railroads cut rates below the trucking rate in a specific area, either the trucks in that area are put out of business or else they have to meet the rail rates. The result is a net loss of revenue for the railroads. Perhaps that is one of the reasons we are now having to subsidize the rates as we are being asked to do by this resolution.
Here is a particular instance in British Columbia as outlined in a submission made by a tariff agent for the trucking industry in British Columbia. This case illustrates the necessity for the trucking industry being allowed to appear as an interested party before the board of transport commissioners when hearings are held. This brief has been submitted to the board of transport commissioners, along with a request for a hearing, and I have been informed since that the board has turned down this request. I do not want to get into too much detail here, so I am just going to give you a general picture. Before the railroads asked for their 17 per cent increase the rate charged by both rail and truck transportation was $1.20 per hundred pounds for this particular haul. When the 17 per cent increase in rail rates went into effect the rail rate went up to $1.40 per hundred pounds. The trucking industry, which was having its own difficulties in getting along on the rates being charged, applied to the public utilities commission in British Columbia for a 17 per cent increase so that the rates would still be competitive. However, the public utilities commission did not grant the full 17 per cent in this particular instance. They granted the trucking industry only 8.5 per cent. The trucking industry accepted this for the moment and prepared to fight the case for the second 8.5 per cent.
In the meantime the railroads reduced their rates down to $1.10 per hundred pounds. Surely, if there was any need to reduce them

Freight Rates
there was no need to reduce them below what the trucks were charging because that certainly resulted in a net loss of revenue to the railroads. As I pointed out before, the obvious thing that is going to occur is that the trucking industry will meet these rates. The net result will be that the railroads will have a loss of revenue without a net gain in traffic. This is another factor in the freight rate situation which is facing us now, and may be one of the reasons we are being asked to subsidize rail operations.
If I may sum up, I should like to impress upon the government once again my hope that whatever commission is going to be set up it will be one which will investigate fully the impact of the trucking industry in all its aspects, for-hire truckers, people operating their own trucks or U-drive trucks, upon the freight rate structure.
I firmly believe that it should be done in complete co-operation with the provinces. Before a commission is empowered to undertake this investigation I believe there should be consultation with the provinces to cover the aspect and to see if some agreement cannot be reached, to investigate whether trucks across Canada as a whole are paying their fair share of the taxes and to see whether trucks are paying too low a rate in some areas are not making rates sufficiently low in those areas and thereby causing the railroads to put their rates too high in other parts of the country.

Mr. Chairman, this subject of freight rates is of vital importance to my constituency. I should therefore like to give a few facts and figures which are pertinent to our economy. Now that the Minister of Transport has arrived on this side of the house I am sure we will get what we ask for.
I am in receipt of several communications from various lakehead firms objecting very strenuously to any freight rate increase for northwestern Ontario. These letters also demonstrate the alarm that is felt in connection with the so-called "alleviation of discrimination" in how the proposed $20 million subsidy will be applied. If northwestern Ontario is not given the same measure of consideration which is being given to the western provinces it could mean, not only hardship to the people of northwestern Ontario but also a terrific burden to many of our firms and industries.
The failure of the province of Ontario to join the other eight provinces in protest against these freight rate increases for the people living in the northwestern part of the province, which is approximately 1,000 miles

from Toronto, is the proof that the government of Ontario is not really much concerned with its welfare. It is again an unchallenged reminder that northwestern Ontario should have been a part of Manitoba, as it is generally conceded that the interests of that part of the province are clearly more closely linked with the prairie provinces by reason of the fact that the lakehead is the transshipping point for grain, iron ore and general merchandise.
I could not do better justice to the subject than to quote a few paragraphs from a file of correspondence in support of government consideration of measures which will ensure a fair deal for northwestern Ontario. I have a letter from the general manager of the Northwestern Ontario development association which reads in part as follows:
Announcement was made recently by the federal government that it plans to appoint a special body to review the general field of rail problems and freight rates. Also announced was the intention to undertaken a study "to work out measures to relieve against inequities in the freight rate structure."
According to press reports emanating from Ottawa, serious consideration looms of a more favourable freight rates deal for the four western and four Atlantic provinces. In the middle province of Ontario, the problem confronting our northwestern economy is obvious.
The recent 17 per cent freight rate boost, unopposed by Ontario, placed an additional heavy burden on our northwestern industries, business firms and consumers. The railways have announced their intention of applying for a further rate increase.
Our association, with other regional bodies, is endeavouring to compile a fund of information and evidence to support whatever representations might be made later in behalf of our area to the proper authorities.
If we are left outside the areas to which concessions might be granted in any freight rates overhaul, the disadvantages to our existing economy would be serious and our prospects for continued growth dealt a damaging blow.
Only the other day I received the following telegram from the chairman of the joint transport committee of the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur:
Unless proposed freight rates subsidization offers northwestern Ontario same assistance as Manitoba discrimination should be charged.
I have here a communication from one of the large departmental stores. It reads in part as follows:
We learned that there may be consideration given a request by all provinces, excepting Quebec and Ontario, which would have the effect of eliminating all or part of the last (17 per cent) freight increase. We are in sympathy with Manitoba's views, but we are deeply concerned about the problem of cost differential which our company would face on goods entering our area from Manitoba. And we know that in order to be competitive, we must make every effort to appeal that the same concession apply to northwestern Ontario.

We handle in excess of $7 million at retail,- a large percentage of this volume comes from operating branch stores in the following locations:

I believe you know that transportation cost hits our type of business heavily, because thousands of small lot shipments are involved. Also, it is necessary to redistribute the bulk of our merchandise from Fort William to our branch stores. This further increases our transportation cost.

Then again I have received several others. I do not wish to read them all. I have one here in particular concerning a large hardware store also located at the lakehead. It reads as follows:
We are writing you in connection with the proposed increase in freight rates, particularly west of the lakehead.
We are given to understand that manufacturers in the east can ship to wholesalers, such as ourselves, in Winnipeg, at the old freight rate, both in carload and l.c.l. shipments. We also understand that they are able to ship from Winnipeg back to Ontario at the old freight rate.
On the other hand, we understand that on shipments from manufacturers in the east to distributors, such as ourselves in the lakehead, we are forced to pay the increased freight rate. When we ship to places such as Dryden, Kenora, Fort Frances, and Atikokan, we are charged the new increased freight rate.
If this information is correct, we wish to offer a very strong objection, for to us this is rank discrimination. We have already run into a situation with one of our competitors in Winnipeg shipping nails to Atikokan at a much cheaper price than we can offer, shipping from the lake-head. We have no way of knowing whether these are imported nails, which are considerably cheaper, or whether the above freight rate structure affects this price. This is just one item that we can think of at the moment. This could also apply to other lines of hardware.
We would certainly appreciate you taking this matter up with the transport board, and register our strong objection.
Then there is another one which says:
The situation here can be put briefly, but is, nevertheless, extremely serious. Our company operated during 1958 at a new loss of $557,488.73 and during this time we paid out $988,689.35 in freight charges. These charges of course were at the old rates before the 17 per cent increase. 66968-9-146i

As can be seen from the above, any freight increase is an extreme hardship to us and further increases are beyond all reason. We are beginning to wonder how long it will take to squeeze us out of business.
I trust that the above will be of some help to you. Should you require further information by all means get in touch with me again.
Then there are others, but I do not wish to take up the time of the committee in dealing with all this correspondence which I have received. Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take any more than a few minutes of the time of the committee; nevertheless I want to express a view which I offer not as a solution but as a suggestion. In making it I do so because we have had many members express concern over the problem of the rate structure as it affects many areas of Canada, particularly those hon. members represent. I think it is hardly necessary for me to point out that the rate structure as such reveals some inequality of rates, which perhaps penalize the area which I represent more than any other section of Canada, and thus I am also concerned. The problem is indeed acute. I think the point which we must remember, however, is that it is going to become a great deal more acute unless the action which has been suggested by the hon. minister is taken and acted on, because it has been indicated to us by the railways that in the next fifteen years they are going to require about a billion and a third dollars. These dollars are to be used purely for replacement costs and the extension of new services. So that while the situation is critical today, and we have a history of going from one crisis to another and from one increase in the rate structure to yet another, each of these adjustments has not altered the position nor has it attacked the problem at its source.
The source of the problem is to put somehow the railways on a paying basis. That is not just a pious hope; it has to be effected, otherwise, as previous members have indicated, we will never reach a solution either temporary or permanent. Therefore I think we should first of all recognize the need for the subsidy which has been indicated in the resolution, and while we can state that we oppose subsidies, it is intended by the government only as a stopgap until such time as the whole problem can be dealt with. This, it has been clearly indicated, will be

Freight Rates
followed by the royal commission and any action recommended by that commission will follow in due course.
I have said that the railways indicate to us that they are going to have to undertake very sizeable capital expenditures. These amount to about $83 million a year. Therefore, if we are going to attack the source of the problem, we are going to have to provide for them a source of revenue in addition to the ordinary operating revenues which as a corporation they receive. I think then it is essential that the commission recognize, as the government does now, that the next ten years are going to be more difficult than the past, because the call on our railways to meet the demands for new services and the need for the replacement of present equipment has never been as extreme as it will be in the coming years.
The suggestion that I have made is that a capital fund should be established by the government which would operate on a revolving basis over the next ten-year period, and on which the railways would be permitted to draw at a nominal low interest rate. That would get them over the hump so that they would not be required to come back repeatedly for increases in freight rates just to make temporary adjustments, thus delaying the eventual day of reckoning. I suggest that the capital fund if established would not be unlike a partial solution which the United States has followed in offering to the railways guaranteed loans to meet exactly the same situation. They have taken this positive action together with reducing services to certain areas where the railways have been asked to operate, for which there is little desire by the community and very little hope of any practical revenue being derived by the railways concerned.
I believe, then, in summary, that in order to place the railways on a paying basis it is not sufficient merely to adjust the inequalities in the freight structure but rather we are going to have to meet the costs of operation which cannot be met by current revenues. I suggest that a capital grant to the extent of about $30 million during the initial period, on the basis which I have suggested, would meet the urgent demand, thus endeavouring to attack the source rather than make, as I have said, a temporary adjustment. That is the one thought which I have with respect to the monetary aspect of the problem.
I also have two other suggestions. The first is a subject which has been mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway dealing with competitive transportation, and in particular motor transport which serves and connects the various provinces in Canada. It does seem to me that we are going to have
[Mr. Smith (Calgary South) .1
to come to the day when we must place all competing forms of transportation under one administrative body to determine the relationship of the tariffs which they charge in competition with one another. It seems inconsistent to me to have a competitive system where one means of transportation is kept under a fairly tight rein, examined and made responsible by the government of Canada as a public convenience, and the other is left completely without any form of control. I have noticed a growing desire amongst the transport companies themselves to see at least that their rates are published on a federal basis, because they are not concerned, funnily enough, with the competition of the railways but are concerned with the competition of those who undercut in their the competition of those who undercut in their own business of transport. So I see a need for a different approach to bring about regulations which will relate one competitive mode of transport and another in their respective rate structures.
The third suggestion I offer is directed to the old problem of agreed charges. These are charges which are made between the railway company and the shipper whereby he agrees to ship a high volume, up to 80 per cent, of his traffic through the particular railway concerned. It was designed in a special instance to compete with certain other forms of transportation, mainly by water, and I think this is paradoxical inasmuch as it eliminates competition, especially as far as truckers are concerned. I think we should examine the agreed charge system carefully, because to a large extent it has increased the cost of transportation, certainly into the prairies. It is an established fact that in many instances it is possible to ship products from eastern Canada to Calgary cheaper via Vancouver than by shipping them to Calgary direct. I maintain that agreed charges have not served the purpose which they were intended to serve. This is an area which should receive close scrutiny in an effort to deal with the source of the problem. Nothing else will be sufficient. Unless we succeed in meeting this problem the entire financial structure of the railways could collapse around them. It is therefore of vital importance to find some constructive solution to the problem of how they are going to meet their very extensive costs over the next 10-year period.

Mr. Chairman, before this resolution passes I should like to direct a question or two to the Minister of Transport. I understood him to say the other night that shipments across the international boundary line between Canada and the United States would not be subject to the increase in freight rates. I would point out that shipments from

Michigan, and particularly shipments of farm products, get the benefit of a cheaper rate to Toronto than do farm products from the Windsor area in Canada, and I should like to know from the minister whether or not the increase in freight rates will give United States farmers any further advantage in connection with getting their products to Toronto and to other Canadian markets.
Another thing which has been brought to my notice is the fact that Canadian farmers can ship to points in eastern Canada-to Montreal for instance-from the Essex-Kent area by routing their shipments by way of Detroit. These products are carried by United States railways to Montreal and points east. I should like to ask the minister to comment on this aspect of the question.

Just before the minister comments on the statement made by the hon. member for Welland, I should like to join with him in asking the minister to give consideration to the question which has just been put to him because it is a very serious one for the farmers of southwestern Ontario.
Undoubtedly the interest of the hon. member for Welland in this matter arises from the fact that he was born in the district and, more particularly, that he joined with a number of us during the Easter weekend in giving consideration to some aspects of this very problem. The increase in freight rates does seem to give United States farmers-farmers in Michigan, for example-an advantage over farmers in Essex or in Kent-corn growers or soybean growers in both jurisdictions-and if the advantage is as great as it would appear to be, the situation is undoubtedly a very serious one. The question implied by the hon. member for Welland is this: is it not a fact that a farmer in the state of Michigan, for instance, is able to ship corn or soybeans in competition with the Canadian growers into Canada over Canadian railroads with an advantage denied to Canadian farmers as a result, in this instance, of the increase in freight rates?
This situation is, I know, not one which arises as of yesterday, although the particular situation which does confront the farmers in this district is one which is accentuated as a result of the increase in freight rates to which the government acceded a few months ago. The situation is, of course, serious in its basic quality. It is possible for farmers to ship corn from Chicago to points in Canada cheaper than it is possible for Canadian corn growers or Canadian soybean growers to ship those commodities to various points in Canada from a Canadian point of origin.
Freight Rates
If this action of the government will lead to a settlement or a resolution of the long term problem which I have just mentioned, or of the short term one created by the increase in freight rates, there will be much satisfaction. In any event I strongly support the implication of the question put by the hon. member for Welland as to whether or not something can be done immediately to take care of the discrimination which now exists and which allows such preferential treatment of United States farmers as opposed, say, to farmers in Essex and Kent who are confronted with the burden of these increased freight rates.
There is also, of course, the long term question of being able to ship United States farm products from points in the United States into Canada cheaper than they can be shipped from points in Ontario such as Kent and Essex to other points in Canada. It seems to me that the whole question of the depressed state of agriculture in this particular section is in a large measure attributable to the defects of the freight rates structure. This might be an appropriate moment for the government to take a second look at the whole problem and try to bring relief to thousands of farmers in southwestern Ontario, notably in the counties of Essex and Kent.

I was hoping that the minister would answer some of the questions put to him as we went along, but I will give him a few more to answer later.
The minister obviously feels, since he has tried to repeat his original statement several times, that it is a model of clarity. I have gone over this statement, and this model of clarity makes very little sense. I took home with me copies of the debates on this subject which occupied the house just before the recess and gave them to a couple of acquaintances of mine who are the only people in our area, I would say, who are knowledgeable on the question of freight rates. I asked one of them for his comments afterwards, and he said: "It seems to me that most of the people in the House of Commons who speak on freight rates are boobs." I said: "Well, it is a very complicated topic and you must understand we are just amateurs at this sort of thing." He said: "Yes, but it seems to me that the biggest boob is the Minister of Transport, and he is the man who is supposed to have a policy on it."
What hits me about this statement is that I do not think the minister wrote it. I think it was written for him, and I think that is one of the reasons he sticks so closely to it. I do not think the minister understands much about what this interim policy is going to

Freight Rates
mean any more than we do, and I think there are some questions which should be answered before this is referred to the committee.
This is one of the techniques employed by the minister. He appeared to say, "Let us get this thing to the committee where we will have all the technical people and all your questions will be answered in detail." My experience in committees, which is admittedly brief, has been that when we get to the committee with all the experts very soon we poor amateur boobs, the members of this house, quickly find ourselves out of our depth. While we are in this committee and amongst our peers-especially our peer the Minister of Transport-I think this is the time when we should have the preliminary exposition as to what the interim policy will be.
I should like to know from the minister how this will apply in an area way. Will we land in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines and find that we have representatives there from eight provinces, each representative stating his case, or will we have to ferret out from the representatives of the minister exactly how it will bear provincially or on a regional basis? These are some of the things I think we should know from this statement.
I should like to know what the minister meant by the statement he made on March 24 in introducing this resolution as reported at page 2207 of Hansard of that date:
The government has decided that the most effective relief is to be afforded by confining the subsidy to a reduction in the non-competitive class and commodity rates, including the joint rail-water rates which are differentially related to the rail rates. These rates are generally known as "normal" rates, and are the ones which have taken the full percentage increases authorized by the board over many years.
I should like to have a simple exposition of that statement. I would like a fuller explanation of what is meant by rates which are differentially related to rail rates and what is meant by normal rates. I should like to have the explanation made right here and now. Beyond that I should like to know how this subsidy will affect the bridge subsidy or if it will affect it at all. I think the minister knows what I mean by the bridge subsidy. We have never been able to figure out how it affects northern Ontario. All we know is that we have the highest freight rates in Canada. We are interested in finding out about the regional basis of the application of this measure because we wonder if we are going to be lumped with the west.
In one of his off-the-cuff statements in which I assume he would be more frank than usual the minister indicated that if British

Columbia suffered the most it would gain the most from this subsidy. I should like to have a fuller explanation of what he meant by that. We in northern Ontario feel that we have suffered. I feel it is about time we had a clear exposition.
When hon. members got back from the Easter vacation we discovered the usual number of briefs and representations in the mail. I just enjoyed reading the submission of the Canadian lumber association to the cabinet committee on freight rates. In essence the brief represented a call for the repeal of the Crowsnest pass rates. In the same mail I discovered a pamphlet published by the Alberta wheat pool called "The Crowsnest Pass Agreement in Review", which is a very clear exposition of why we maintain these rates.
Several hon. members have spoken about the position of the trucking industry. Probably the minister has looked at some of the material contained in The Motor Carrier, a magazine that represents the interests of the trucking people. I was particularly intrigued by the headline I found on one page which read:
Subsidy Issue Sparks Dramatic Cabinet Cloak and Dagger Affair
It is not difficult to imagine our dashing minister involved in a cabinet cloak and dagger affair of some kind or other. What I would like to know is what recognition will be given in this interim period to the position advanced by the truckers? They are dead set against this subsidy. Let us have an explanation from the minister as to how this subsidy is going to apply fairly to the railways and not apply unfairly to their competitors, the trucking people. In effect that is what was asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I think we merit from the minister at this time something much better than the exposition he has given us.
The whole purpose of the minister's exposition seemed to be, "Let us get this to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines." To my way of thinking that is not the place for a clear outline of how this legislation is going to apply for the next year. I believe the place for that is right here and now in this committee. I was pleased to find that my opinion in this regard is identical with that of the hon. member for Laurier. Doubtless the minister will recognize that some of us over here in our opinions do not always dovetail with the opinions of the hon. member for Laurier but this is a case where we are in agreement in feeling that this statement is not good enough. We need a clear, concise outline of how this legislation will work in this one-year period.

I should like to say that I think that we have had enough of royal commissions especially those set up to inquire into freight rates and transportation. I feel it is about time this government took advantage of the knowledge of the board of transport commissioners and of the findings of previous royal commissions and demonstrated two things, some leadership and some guts, in nailing down a national transportation policy without resorting to another royal commission which will take an interminable amount of time to report and is almost certain not to have the authority to consider all the problems relating to the question. Royal commissions do serve a purpose but I feel that sometimes we campaign too frequently to have them set up. In this case the government should show leadership with respect to a national policy on transportation and freight rates rather than shoving the question into one of these corners. The present record of the government with respect to royal commissions is not really an enchanting picture if we look at the various royal commissions that have been established and consider the great length of time it has taken them to getting around to making even interim reports and the fact that there seems to be some lack of agreement on interpreting just what their findings mean.
I do not see how the idea of the establishing of a royal commission to study this question could excite anybody except perhaps the lawyers who will make a killing presenting the cases for the various provinces in connection with the freight rate aspect of the question. If the minister really digs into the transportation and freight rate problems and gets down to work-
