subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill C-19, to amend the Criminal Code (corporal punishment).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have the privilege of introducing this bill which deals specifically with the abolition and removal from the Criminal Code of the provision for whipping, a provision which calls specifically for the use as so described in the Criminal Code of a weapon-I think it can only be properly described as a weapon-known as the cat-o'-nine-tails. This is a device which is not
Criminal Code
normally seen by Canadian citizens today unless they happen to be watching late movies such as Mutiny on the Bounty, the Corsican Brothers and others. Vivid in my mind, as I am sure in the minds of many other members also, are scenes where human beings are flogged, in some cases flogged to death.
The arguments in favour of the abolition of corporal punishment follow a pattern very similar to that in the case of the arguments established in support of the abolition of capital punishment. They deal specifically with the aspect of a deterrent and the fact as no doubt will be established by speakers from other parties in the house, that there is no evidence, statistically or otherwise to support the retention of corporal punishment. The argument that corporal punishment, whipping in particular, is motivated by revenge is, of course, true. We have all heard people discussing a certain crime that has been committed and making the statement that hanging or whipping is too good for the person who committed the offence. When this subject has come up in private conversation I have often asked people who have made such statements what they would prefer to do. In most cases they go further than the use of that unhappy device, the cat-o'-nine-tails, as a means of torture to extract revenge and suggest some of the ancient oriental methods but finally before we reach drawing and quartering they concede my point.
There are morbid aspects of corporal punishment which disturb me as a member of parliament no more or less than they disturbed me as a private citizen. You, Mr. Speaker, I, every member of the house and each and every member of our society has a hand on the whip when a whipping takes place in the same way that we have a hand on the rope in the case of a hanging. We as citizens of Canada and members of the house are elected specifically to enact such legislation as truly reflects the feelings and instincts of the people we represent.
In the case of corporal punishment the same risk of error is involved, although I grant not to the same extent, as in the case of capital punishment. If a man is hanged and evidence is later discovered indicating that the accused was in fact innocent, nothing can be done, but I submit there is permanent damage to the recipient of corporal punishment in that the man carries the marks of it to his grave.
The debate concerning corporal punishment has raged in many countries of the world for many years and in a few the use of the whip or lash has been abolished for over 100 years. There has been a trend in

Criminal Code
human behaviour and human conscience reflected in the legislatures and laws of many lands which tends toward what I like to think is an enlightened point of view regarding corporal punishment.
Not too many weeks ago I saw in a popular pictorial magazine a series of pictures of a thief who had been apprehended in one of the Middle Eastern countries. The picture was taken by a man who had secreted a camera into the area. The sequence of pictures showed a poor man, a beggar, being dragged into the public square and held down by three or four other men while a policeman cut off a hand. The last picture showed the man minus his hand sitting in front of his hovel and the hand that had been cut off was nailed to the doorway of his abode. The final comment in the story accompanying the picture was that some of those who had their hands removed had died. Yet burglary continues in that country. I have read a discussion of corporal punishment in "The History of Corporal Punishment" by George Ryley Scott and in his book he describes the action of the cat-o'-nine-tails. I tried to obtain and bring to this house this afternoon a cat-o'-nine-tails. I have no reason to believe that the present day version differs substantially in structure or effect from the original. I should like to quote briefly from the book to which I have referred in order to give the house some idea of the specific effects of the cat-o'-nine-tails, provision for the use of which is found in our Criminal Code. The author has this to say at page 83:
The English cat-o'-nine-tails, the weapon employed, was a terrible instrument of flagellation. It was a close rival of the Russian knout. The "cat" consisted-
I understand it still does.
-of nine separate thongs of leather or thick whipcord, each two feet in length, and knotted in three places. At each stroke the thongs cut through the skin like so much paper, the knots tearing out lumps of flesh. The sensation of the whipped individual, says Shipp, is "as though the talons of a hawk were tearing the flesh off the bones," and, as stroke follows stroke, and the "cat" becomes clotted with blood, it "falls like a mass of lead upon the back."
This, Mr. Speaker, seems to be a voice from the distant past, something that one might find in such a novel as Mutiny on the Bounty. Yet today in our Criminal Code we find this same instrument, this same weapon, prescribed.
The matter of sadism so far as this subject is concerned is very pertinent and relevant in at least three aspects. Before going into this part of the argument, I should like to give you a definition which I heard of a sadist. A sadist is defined as someone who is kind to a masochist. While this definition

may have a humorous connotation, it leads into an aspect of the punishment which concerns the recipient of flagellation. It has been, I think, demonstrated in studies made of certain aspects of sexual crimes that, far from being a punishment for certain types of such crimes, the whip is possibly a most desirable form of experience for that individual.
Sadism most certainly can occur in the application of the sentence. A judge meting out a sentence, trying by some method to come to the correct number of lashes which might suit a particular crime, has the effectiveness taken out of his decision according to the degree of physical strength and sadistic inclination which may exist in the mind of the individual who is handling the lash. Finally, Mr. Speaker, I submit that sadism is a natural reaction in the minds of society, particularly on the part of those closely associated with a specific crime, but is certainly not something of which we as citizens of Canada today can be proud to find in our laws and in the designated penalties attached thereto.
There is another aspect of this question which many of my colleagues in the house, as I have mentioned, will be discussing. I should like to quote briefly from the chapter headed "Summing-up the Position" in this book on the History of Corporal Punishment which deals with the fears presumed to be part of the deterrent which applies and results from the retention of corporal punishment. The author says:
But the fear Induced by corporal punishment belongs primarily to none of these categories. It is essentially and pre-eminently the fear of physical pain. It is the fear inevitably associated with suffering of a degrading, deliberate and debasing nature. Fear which is associated with and restricted to physical pain, as a punitive factor, possesses no true reformative power. Thus the qualities which commended corporal punishment to primitive and savage races, and which still provide strong justification for its employment by the individual as a means of exacting private vengeance, become indefensible as applicable to any penological system of the modern state.
Later on the author refers to another aspect of it which I should like to quote.
In many quarters the fear has been expressed that the abolition of the "cat" and the birch would lead to an increase in the incidence of crime. There is no justification for any such contention.
Historically, as the demand has been made for the removal of the more severe forms of punishment, the cry has gone out that if this is removed there will be a flood of crime. Nobody will be safe in his bed. Finally, when enlightened governments have taken action to reduce the bestiality in our penalty sections those fears, so vigorously expressed, have proven to be unfounded. The abolition of

corporal punishment for women and girls did not lead to any increase in crime amongst the female population.
One of the most powerful and most convincing arguments against any form of corporal punishment is that the sentence which the judge or magistrate may consider merely adequate will be transformed, by those responsible for its application, into a brutal attack or the severest torture reminiscent of some of the days of the Spanish inquisition. These, Mr. Speaker, are some of the reasons why those of us who favour the abolition of corporal punishment are supporting this bill.
There is a further reason, of course, contained in the report of the committee of the Senate and House of Commons which reported on this matter in 1956. I am quoting from page 47 of the final report of that committee, paragraph 27:
Accordingly, the committee recommends that corporal punishment be abolished for any of the offences for which it is presently prescribed in the Criminal Code.
The broader aspects of the reform of our penal system, which I understand are receiving most active consideration at the present time by the government, must embody some other set of principles, principles which will result in remedy, reform and rehabilitation rather than extracting what I submit are the outmoded, savage penalties presently prescribed in the Criminal Code.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity of speaking for a few minutes in support of the bill which has been introduced by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee), asking this house to pass an amendment to abolish corporal punishment as part of a judicial sentence in Canada. It is rather extraordinary, and to our shame, that Canada is one of the few countries in the world that still retains the lash and the paddle as part of a judicial sentence. I can only express the hope that hon. members of this house who have to deal with matters of law can visit or will visit our institutions and ascertain just what takes place there. I am certain that almost every person who has been inside a penal institution and has seen the lash and the paddle used, or who have been informed how they are administered, could never stand in his place in this house and oppose the abolition of the lash or the paddle.
May I just take a few minutes to explain the procedure to those who are keenly interested in this question, and tell them just what that means. When a person who receives a judicial sentence of the lash or paddle, in accordance with the order of the court, the 66968-9-147
Criminal Code
warden of the penitentiary has to carry out that order. The inmate in prison is taken down to a small room in the basement of the penitentiary. The lash, as was pointed out by the mover of this bill, is sometimes known as the cat-o'-nine-tails. I disagree with only one statement that he made. It is different from the book he quoted. It is now eight lengths of nylon cord. They have modernized it to that extent. It is now nylon cord.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, the inmate is taken into a small room. If it is the lash, there is a table sloping at a 30 degree angle up against the wall. At the end of that table embedded in the concrete are steel plates. The feet of the inmate are fastened by leather straps to the steel plates in the concrete so that he cannot move. He is then stretched along the inclined board, with arms extended, and his arms are strapped to the board so as to be completely immovable. He is stripped to the waist.
Then, Mr. Speaker, in case you have never seen that procedure, may I tell you that a leather belt is put around the kidneys because a blow on the kidneys can kill. Then the man who is strapped there, his feet on the floor, his arms extended, with protection so that he cannot be killed, with a leather belt over the kidneys, gets in Canada what is known as the lash. I want to tell you Mr. Speaker, that I have personally visited penal institutions in Canada where a man has been ordered the lash by a court, and I have seen men in hospital with their backs wrecked by the lash seven days after they received it.
If the order is not for the lash it is for the paddle. Although it is called the paddle, actually it is the strap. The strap varies in Canada according to the institution. It does not vary in length nor width nor thickness but it varies as to whether or not it has any holes in it. About half the institutions use a strap called the paddle with holes. The difference in the administration of that form of punishment is that instead of being on a sloping form-their feet are still strapped to steel plates to the floor-they are bent over a table with their arms outstretched and the leather belts holding their arms. The trousers are down. The leather belt is over the kidneys. Then the paddle is administered. It is bad enough without the holes. But if the leather belt has the holes in it, the flesh is lacerated. There, too, Mr. Speaker, I have seen these men in hospital.
We do not forget the crimes of these mei but we should give consideration to the purpose of their punishment. Surely we in Canada have now reached a point of understanding of modern penology to realize that the purpose is not a matter of revenge but for the protection of society. It is an answer

Criminal Code
that they are obliged to give to the people for an anti-social act. But I believe- especially from knowing the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton)-in the application of education in an endeavour to rehabilitate.
I have long had an interest in penology. About five years ago I visited a penitentiary and I asked the warden if he would call into his office everyone he knew of in that institution who had received the lash or the paddle either as a judicial punishment or as part of a discipline under the authority of the warden's court and the warden did so. That afternoon the warden and I together interviewed right in the institution some 17 men, I think it was, who in their criminal life had had the lash or the paddle. They were told to speak absolutely bluntly. It is all on the record.
The warden said, "This is Mr. Harold E. Winch, M.P. and he wants to ask you some questions." So in turn we questioned every inmate. We asked, "Are you a better man because of corporal punishment?" "What is your reaction to corporal punishment?" "Is it a detriment to further crime or to breaking the law of the institution?" "Has it made you a better boy or a better man?" Sixteen of them said no and one said yes. It was most interesting, Mr. Speaker, that one chap said "It almost made a murderer out of me." He said, "The first time I ever received corporal punishment was when I was at a reformatory in Ontario, and I got the paddle because I broke the law in the reformatory; I had one dollar in my pocket and I was not supposed to have any money. After what happened," he said, "I swore I would get that man." He escaped from the reformatory and he and a chum went across the border. They stole a car, stole a gun and came back. This boy told me-and the warden can confirm what I say-that he had had the man that gave him the paddle in the sights of that rifle. However, luckily for him, his chum woke up to what was taking place and removed it. That is one experience I had along with the warden in talking to those in the institution.
The hon. member for York-Scarborough mentioned the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons which investigated this matter. Our joint committee had the counsel of that committee, a well-known lawyer of this city, interview in the city of Toronto a number of men who had received the lash or the paddle but who are now out of the institutions. Most of them have been very well established in the business life of the city of Toronto. The members of our committee kept completely away. The interviewing was done only by our counsel, and the report of our counsel

referred to the men only by a letter of the alphabet so that the names of the individuals were kept completely in confidence. I would invite the members of this house to read the transcript of the evidence of that interview with those who have become rehabilitated, some of them prominent in business, and who had had the lash or the paddle. With only two exceptions their replies were that corporal punishment antagonizes a man, makes him bitter and vicious, and more anti-social than when he was sentenced.
Mr. Speaker, there is the matter of the transcript record of the three-year study of the joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate; there is the record from such authority as that quoted by the mover of this bill; and there is my own experience. But may I just add one other word and it is this. In a few days or weeks this house will be asked to pass millions of dollars for the maintenance of penitentiaries in this country, millions of dollars for the maintenance of police forces in this country. All that money comes out of the taxpayers' pockets. As I said before, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) I am sure has in mind modern methods of rehabilitation, not crocodile tears or simply retention and education. Surely when we recognize the cost of keeping a man in a penitentiary, which is I think $4.70 a day, it must be the hope of the government, the minister and the members of this house that when these men are released from the penitentiary they shall not return. We spend, as I say, millions of dollars every year, and we are going to vote millions of dollars inside the next few weeks for the following twelve months to try to rehabilitate those who have proven themselves anti-social.
Mr. Speaker, in nearly every penitentiary across this country now we have wardens of course, doctors, psychologists, psychiatrists and educationalists, and we are teaching the inmates vocations. If by judicial sentence we have a continuation of what is still the law in this country when the judge orders the lash or the paddle, I am afraid that the money spent in providing the educators, the psychologists and psychiatrists is wasted when a man is strapped and has his back lacerated or his pants taken down and his backside lacerated. It just does not seem to make sense.
But in particular I want to emphasize the absolute stupidity of some of the judges who give a sentence of lashes in two sections; one shortly after the prisoner is admitted to jail and then later before he comes out, so that all that work done by the educationalists, the vocational training men and the doctors is ruined because of the law as it stands today. I am certain from personal interviews, studies and my knowledge of this question that the

bill which is now before us is a bill which demands worthy consideration of all the members of this house, and I sincerely hope that we will wipe this blot off Canada's name and cease to be one of the few remaining countries of the world to use the lash and the paddle as part of a judicial sentence. We do not want to see, because of the approach to this problem of the Minister of Justice and the government, the taxpayers' money being sent down the drain. I hope that this bill which has been introduced many times now will receive the vote of all members of all parties in this House of Commons.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to second the bill proposed by my hon. friend from York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee). Only a week ago it seems we were on opposite sides of the fence on a somewhat similar bill involving capital punishment. I had some reservations about that question, but I have no reservations about the fact that my hon. friend through his fine argument presented this afternoon, backed up by the persuasive emotionalism of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), is on the right track. I hope in my own modest way to produce some statistics for the attention of the house which will support the conclusions which have been reached by both those hon. members, and also the conclusions which have been reached in other countries in the world which have decided to abolish this particular method of punishment.
But first, sir, may I be permitted to examine two arguments that will probably be used by those who are in favour of retaining this particular form of punishment. The first one is probably best expressed by that old master of the English law, William Blackstone, Oxford's first Vinerian professor of law:
Of all parts of a law the most effectual is the vindicatory. For it is but lost labour to say, "Do this, avoid that", unless we also declare, "This shall ^ be the consequence of your non-compliance." We must therefore observe that the main strength and force of a law consists in the penalty annexed to it. Herein is to be found the principal obligation of human laws.
This, Mr. Speaker, may be a persuasive argument at first blush, but I suggest to the house that this argument contains a fallacy, and that is that there are other methods of punishment available for offenders quite apart from the inhumane one of corporal punishment. The other punishment available is simply the threat or the actuality of imprisonment.
The second argument that might be used to maintain the present situation comes from the old adage, "Spare the rod and spoil the

This is a wonderful field for professional and amateur psychologists, and anyone who has seen children in action or been a child himself, which takes in everybody, has a wonderful opportunity to vent his or her personal opinion on this philosophy. But again, I think that to spare the rod and spoil the child has no particular application to this argument. For one thing, the child in the home loves the parent and expects the parent to assert a certain amount of discipline. The child also knows that if the parent is forced to take drastic measures, such as a spanking, if it is done out of a love for the child, while the child's love might abate for the moment under the stings of the punishment, it will return in full force and be strengthened by respect.
On the other hand, in the penal institutions of this country, Mr. Speaker, it is very unlikely that any of the inmates love the warden or that the warden, for that matter, loves the inmates, and the imposition of the rod under such circumstances would not be accompanied by the factors which play such a vital role in the home, namely the factors of love and affection and the need for children to be obedient to their parents. I hope in those short words that I have helped dispose of two of the arguments that will probably be used by those who favour the retention of corporal punishment.
Now for the matter of the statistical argument. Does it work anyway? This was considered before the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons in 1954. I have their report and I shall read very briefly from it if I may. I do not think the statistics given that committee by the Canadian authorities are particularly helpful, because the numbers involved are not large enough. Then I will go on to quote some of the findings of a committee in the United Kingdom which dealt with a much larger number of offenders, and I think I can prove statistically beyond all reasonable doubt to even the most sceptical in this House of Commons that there really is no merit in retaining the use of the lash or the strap. As to the Canadian picture, it will be found at page 781 of the joint committee's report. Question No. 20 asked:
In your opinion, does corporal punishment operate as a deterrent to (a) the young offender, (b) the recidivist, (c) the sexual offender?
There are answers to this question from several of the western provinces-British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan. There is no comment from Ontario, and some actual figures from the commissioner of penitentiaries. The answer from British Columbia is that there seems to be some evidence of paddling having been useful in helping young

Criminal Code
offenders to redirect their activity. From Saskatchewan, there was the following reply: We know of no evidence to support the view that corporal punishment in fact operates as a deterrent to any group of offenders.
These are, apparently, opinions plucked out of the air by attorneys general or by people in their offices who may be softhearted or hardhearted as the case may be. However, the commissioner of penitentiaries did offer some statistical fodder to the committee. I suppose the main question really is whether the lash, once given, tends to ensure that a person will not repeat his offence, so I do not intend to deal with all the statistics which the commissioner presented to the committee, though I will deal with some of them, those which concern the recidivists. One hundred and ninety three persons were awarded corporal punishment who had previously served sentences of imprisonment in the period from January 1, 1943 to December 31, 1953. I myself had a very interesting interview with a recidivist a few weeks ago. This recidivist had recidivisted time and time again, because he had spent 10 different terms in Canadian penitentiaries. It was his opinion, in the light of his studies, that recidivism took place within one year of an offender being released from a penal institution. I think that is significant, for if there is anything about the lash and the strap it should be that the scars and the humiliation and the degradation of undergoing such punishment are still fresh within this period, if not upon the body then on the mind at least of a released prisoner. And yet statistics from Canada supplied by the commissioner of penitentiaries seem to indicate, if they indicate anything at all, that the lash has no particular effect.
May I turn now to what has occurred in the United Kingdom, and I use as my source material a report of the departmental committee on corporal punishment, 1928, issued by Her Majesty's stationery office. This committee had this to say as reported on page 80:
We have given due weight to the opinions which witnesses have expressed to us on this point on the basis of their personal experience; but we thought it desirable to supplement this evidence by obtaining some statistical information regarding the subsequent record of offenders who have been dealt with by means of corporal punishment. Statistics based solely on the subsequent

records of persons sentenced to corporal punishment would be defective in two respects. First, they could not show what the man's subsequent career might have been if he had not been flogged. Secondly, as corporal punishment of adults is always combined with a sentence of imprisonment or penal servitude, they could not show how far the subsequent career may have been influenced by the term of imprisonment or penal servitude. No figures could elucidate these two points completely; but, in order to throw some light on this aspect of the matter, we have obtained figures which enable a comparison to be made between the subsequent record of persons who actually received corporal punishment and of persons who were liable to corporal punishment but were dealt with by other means.
The statistical analysis which the committee presented with the help of the home office and New Scotland Yard was an analysis of the records of 440 persons who were convicted of robbery with violence during the period 1921 to 1930. The report states:
Of the 142 flogged, two have subsequently been convicted of a second offence of robbery with violence, and in a third case a charge of robbery with violence was dropped when the offender was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude on another charge founded on the same facts. Of the 298 who were not flogged, three have since been reconvicted of robbery with violence: but two of these men were mentally unstable and it seems very doubtful whether either of them would have been restrained from committing the second offence if he had been flogged on the first occasion.
And the conclusion which the committee reached was this:
So far as these 440 cases are concerned, it appears that a sentence of imprisonment or penal servitude without corporal punishment was no less effective in deterring the offender from committing a further offence of robbery with violence than a sentence of imprisonment or penal servitude combined with corporal punishment. As regards subsequent offences other than robbery with violence, the record of the men flogged was bound to be worse than that of those who had not been flogged. Of those flogged 55 per cent were subsequently convicted of serious crime, as compared with 43.9 per cent of those not flogged.
I find this report very interesting, and I hope other hon. members will also. I think there is much food for thought in this very fine study which was made in the United Kingdom. The report continues:
It might have been assumed that this would be due to the fact that the persons not flogged included a higher proportion of first offenders who might be less likely to offend again: but when the cases were subdivided into groups according to the previous record of the men concerned it was found that, even among the first offenders, the subsequent record of those flogged was less satisfactory than that of those who were not flogged.
Time is getting on, and there are others who wish to take part in the debate. I think that perhaps I have given enough statistical information to the house at least to knock the props out from under those who would argue

that flogging and the lash do have a beneficial effect and do tend to alter the personality of a prisoner who undergoes this method of punishment.
In conclusion, if I may, I should like to make two more observations. One is that the mere fact of subjecting a human being to the inhumanity of the whip undoubtedly sets a mark of Cain upon that person. If not, it gives him a peculiar stamp in his own circle and sets him apart from ordinary mankind. It may even, in certain circles, tend to make him a heroic figure, a type of outcast beatnik who is given recognition because of the fact that all the forces of society have combined to subject him to the most inhuman of treatment.
If I have any reservations about the bill I think they would only go so far as the matter of prison discipline. Perhaps the lash or some form of physical punishment is necessary in prison. I am not sure about that. Perhaps my hon. friend will deal with it at some future time. I know we are not going to pass this bill this afternoon. Let us be frank about it. I also heard my hon. friend's heartening words that action may be undertaken by the government. Our debate this afternoon will at least serve the useful purpose of bringing this matter again to the attention of the Canadian public and provoking some new thought about what has become in this country a rather fearful and degrading sore on our body politic.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the house that I support this bill. When the Criminal Code was amended in 1954, we entrusted a joint committee of the house and Senate with the responsibility of making appropriate investigations with regard to capital and corporal punishment, and lotteries.
In 1956, the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons reported to us after investigating the abolition of capital punishment. There is, to my mind, no need to quote from the statements by expert witnesses like doctors and others, who were heard before that committee and who repeatedly explained how corporal punishment was applied. Following the evidence heard, the committee came to the conclusion that capital punishment should be abolished. The relevant report was published at that time in the press and we were able to learn the reasons in favour of abolishing the lash as well.
Some of my learned friends opposite have studied the question. The hon. member for Scarborough (Mr. McGee)) gave us some good arguments and the hon. member for
Criminal Code
Halifax (Mr. McCleave) gave lengthy quotations. However, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), who was a member of the committee which studied the abolition of capital punishment, gave us a description of what that punishment is today, of its bad aspects and detrimental consequences, leading up to the conclusion that it should be abolished.
I share the views of those hon. members and I am in favour of abolishing capital punishment. I shall however limit myself to the following two reasons: the effects of capital punishment on the indivdual are very bad. It induces in him the idea of revenge against society and he becomes embittered against his fellow men. As a matter of fact, that measure which was introduced in the middle ages is obsolete today. Moreover, judges in criminal cases no longer sentence anyone to the lash. Why? Because they know of its detrimental effects on those subjected to this punishment.
Then another amendment was made to the Criminal Code which today would justify the abolition of the lash. The amendment was passed several years ago when the penalty of life imprisonment was introduced for individuals known as habitual criminals.
To those who are opposed to the abolition of the corporal punishment and who say: "What about the man who does not want to mend his ways, who is always before the courts, and constantly sent to prison?" We might answer that, after a third charge, the crown in each province may lodge a complaint and prove to the courts that such a man, being recognized as an habitual criminal, could be given a life sentence.
For all those reasons I believe we should now abolish corporal punishment because it is bad for the individual. I believe that, in a society which prides itself on being modern and in an advanced state of civilization, this form of punishment is no longer warranted and I am convinced that if it were eliminated from our statutes, it would be all to the advantage of the individual.

Mr. Chairman, I might take this opportunity to answer the questions asked by hon. members so far in the debate. The hon. member for Fort William asked that the subsidy should not discriminate against northwestern Ontario. I have already said that there will be no discrimination against any province or region. The hon. member for Port Arthur asked, first of all, what normal rates are, what does it mean when rates are differentially related and what effect will the proposed subsidy have on the existing bridge subsidy.
Normal rates are the ones which have taken the full percentage increases authorized by the board and do not include competitive rates. The differentially related rates referred to are the joint rail and water rates and they are lower than all-rail rates. With respect to the hon. member's inquiry whether this measure will affect the bridge subsidy the answer is that this subsidy is in addition to the bridge subsidy and not in substitution for it in any way.
The hon. members for Welland and Essex East referred to rates on agricultural products moving into Canada from Michigan compared with rates from southern Ontario to points in Canada. The reason for the difference is that the United States produce comes in on international rates which in this instance are lower than the local, domestic rates. These local, domestic rates will have the benefit of the subsidy and the international rates will not. If there is still any discrimination the shipper can complain to the board of transport commissioners and have his complaint investigated.
Lastly, the hon. member for Laurier asked what is the formula which the board of transport commissioners will use to distribute the $20 million subsidy. From the discussions I have had with the board I can say that there will be a horizontal reduction in the level of non-competitive class and commodity rates from the 17 per cent increase authorized by the board to approximately 10 per cent, or a 7 per cent reduction. In effect there is no real formula. This is simply the method by which the subsidy will be applied.

minister did not use the term "royal commission". He implied it, and that is exactly what I said earlier when the minister started bobbing up and down in his seat. An article by Harvey Hickey in the Toronto Globe and Mail of April 3, reads in part:
A royal commission will be appointed shortly to examine the whole structure of railway freight rates, Prime Minister Diefenbaker announced today.
Parliament was not in session. According to this press report the Prime Minister made the announcement during the Easter recess. We are now attempting to ascertain the terms under which the royal commission will operate. We have met with no success. We have been told that we will have an opportunity to discuss this question. We have not been told whether it would be in order but the government agreed it would make the announcement so parliament would have a chance to have the order in council before it when hon. members were in committee upon the bill that is to follow this resolution. In other words, it will be before us when we are in committee on another matter. At that time if the chairman should rise and say we cannot discuss the terms of reference of the royal commission because we have to stick to the clauses of the bill, will there be anyone to say that the chairman is not correct?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OP CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, surely the hon. member knows he could not be more out of order than he is at the moment in discussing a royal commission on this resolution?

speechtext:
That is not quite the ground that the minister raised just a moment ago when he accused me of being out of order. My point is that I am in order because the Speaker said we would be in order. The

Speaker has not said he would allow a discussion at a later date which might be ruled out of order.
The Minister of National Revenue should know that the Prime Minister has been discussing this very question. The Prime Minister has been alluding to a royal commission. He said a royal commission would be set up but apparently its terms have not been decided upon. I should like to know if the order in council has been passed. First it was hinted that there would be a royal commission appointed and then an announcement was made during the Easter recess but now we are told it has not been set up. The announcement has been made but the government is looking to the opposition to tell it what the terms of reference should be. The government has been floundering for a long time and well they might seek our advice.
My advice to the government is first of all that it does not need a royal commission. There have been enough royal commissions on this subject. All the government needs to do at this time as far as further increases in freight rates are concerned is to continue the position it took not many months ago that there should be no further increases in freight rates.
I suggest that the government give consideration to amending this resolution. It is possible to amend it provided a cabinet minister other than the Minister of Transport moves the amendment and provided there is a seconder. I suggest it should be amended to provide a subsidy that would roll back the total 17 per cent freight rate increase so there would be no increase at all and particularly in view of the fact the government disallowed the 3.6 per cent increase. That would be much better than this wishy-washy, catch-as-catch-can policy the government is now trying to get away with. The Prime Minister needs help on what the royal commission should be inquiring into and with respect to what it should do. I do not agree that a royal commission is necessary but if that is the policy of the government I suggest the first instruction to be given the royal commission to bring in recommendations that will prevent further increases in freight rates. That is the first thing that should be provided in the terms of reference in the royal commission.
The second instruction given the royal commission should be to bring in suggestions as to how equitable freight rates can be provided in this country. Those are things the commission should be doing, if there must be one at all. It should also be instructed to examine into the balance sheet of the Canadian Pacific railway to see how this railway

has shown low profits on its railway operations when it is in fact making all kinds of profits on its other operations.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that the terms of reference should include the matter of the board of transport commissioners considering all of the profits of the Canadian Pacific railway and not just those profits earned from railway operations. The Canadian Pacific railway is a mammoth corporation with many departments. It pretends to show need as far as its railway operations are concerned but it has very large profits in several fields.
I have in my hand its 1958 annual report and on page 25 there is a statement of "other income". With regard to net earnings from steamships there was a loss of $1,212,571 in that year. Net earnings from hotel, communication and other properties amounted to $481,393. Dividends amounted to $7,943,339. The next item is net income from petroleum rents, royalties, reservation fees and land rents. There is a very large profit of $6,828,123 resulting from land granted to the C.P.R. from the public domain many years ago. Net income from interest amounted to $3,808,428, and the sub-total is $17,848,712. There are the profits of the C.P.R. other than the profits that have been made from railway operations. These are things that should be considered in any inquiry.
Then, as has been mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East, we feel that a royal commission should give consideration to a national transportation policy to serve the needs of the Canadian people. It should consider the efficient operation of the railways and the provision of adequate services. It should discontinue the policy of taking only the railway operations of the C.P.R. as the yardstick in establishing freight rates in this country.
We have had many royal commissions in this connection in the past. We do not need another one today. We need action by the government, action to roll back increases in freight rates, action to prevent further discrimination through horizontal increases in the future. The government should be enunciating its policy and program instead of bringing forward this temporary measure which may provide very little by way of alleviation to the Canadian public.
I do not think this point has been clarified yet and I should like to ask the Minister of Transport or the Prime Minister to say whether or not it is the policy of the government to prevent further increases in freight rates until such time as the report of the royal commission is in the hands of the government. That, at any rate, would be some progress.

May I have another word in connection with the invitation extended by the Prime Minister with reference to suggestions? I do so with great timidity because I know this is a matter of extreme importance but a number of things come to my mind now and I give them to the house, to the government and to the Prime Minister for what they are worth. In the first place, we have already had an excellent royal commission on transportation, and if I remember what the Prime Minister said when he was on this side of the house I think he was very happy when the announcement was made of the personnel of that commission. I think he was also very happy about the recommendations brought down by the Turgeon commission. Be that as it may, there is no doubt that the inquiry conducted by that royal commission with respect to the freight rate structure was one of the most exhaustive that has ever taken place. Therefore, first of all I think that the royal commission to be established should not be asked to go over the same ground covered by the former commission unless there are matters which have intervened between the 1951 report and the position as it obtains today, which need inquiry.
I also think that the royal commission might well give some consideration to a subject which has been discussed in the house so often, namely the impact of horizontal increases on the extremities of our country, on the maritime provinces, on the prairie provinces and on British Columbia. The Prime Minister will remember that when he was on this side of the house he complained very bitterly, and perhaps rightly so, about the impact of horizontal increases. The 17 per cent case has had a very serious effect so far as horizontal increases are concerned. In other words, that judgment has pointed up the discrimination horizontal increases create in the case of the eastern and western provinces. The 7 per cent reduction is simply an alleviation of that difficulty, but not a solution; and therefore I think this is another matter to which the commission might give consideration.
But perhaps the most important matter that I think should be considered is a long term and short term policy for the railways of this country. I am sure that the Minister of Transport and the government do not have the time to deal with matters of this kind. It seems to me that the commission might well be given, as one of its terms of reference, the consideration of the long and short term policy for the railways of Canada.
With reference to the short term policy I can give to the house four matters which might well be considered. The first is this: The railways have always maintained that some passenger services are an unprofitable operation. Should these services be curtailed or should they not? There is no doubt that some of these services should not. Whether or not the commission should be entrusted with consideration of matters of that kind is, of course, for the government to determine. However, it seems to me that since the railways complain so often, not only in statements by the presidents of both railways but in statements before the board of transport commissioners, that some of these are unprofitable operations then perhaps this is a matter which the commission should be considering.
Then, there is the question of the branch lines of the railways. Are unprofitable branch lines to be maintained? There are some branch lines that must of necessity be maintained. There are, I know, in the Canadian National Railways branch lines that are unprofitable. Are they to be continued at the expense of the ratepayer who will, in effect, because of these pay increased freight rates?
There is also the all important question of the dieselization of the railways. Should railways be completely dieselized or should they not? This is an extremely important matter. Again there is a new factor that has come into railway operation recently and that is the piggy-back rates. Should they be maintained? Should the railways be allowed to fully exploit these rates?
There is another matter which I refer to the government and it is a matter which is of particular interest to the western provinces, but more particularly to the province of Alberta than to any other province. I refer to the one and one-third rule. The Prime Minister will recall that the Turgeon commission made a recommendation concerning the one and one-third rule for intermediate territory and that recommendation of the royal commission was implemented by an amendment to the Railway Act. Unfortunately, however, because of a judgment handed

down by the board of transport commissioners the one and one-third rule is practically inapplicable today. It has no force. While it did apply it was, I am told, of tremendous benefit to the intermediate territory, that is the territory to which transcontinental rates do not apply. This is a matter which the royal commission might well consider, as to whether or not it is possible to implement the one and one-third rule and give the benefit to Alberta and intermediate territory which was envisaged by the Turgeon commission.

If I may, and if the Prime Minister will allow me, I should like to refer to the discussion which took place a moment ago. There were some very pertinent statements made by the Prime Minister dealing with freight rates. I should like to bring them to his attention and ask him if he will comment on them. When he was in Saskatoon on February 13, 1958, here is what he had to say with regard to freight rates:
Mr. Diefenbaker said that last year he had criticized general railway freight rate increases as being unfair to the western provinces.
"Did we act?" The government had "help up" a 3.8 per cent railway freight rate increase allowed by the board of transport commissioners earlier this year.

On freight rates, Mr. Diefenbaker spelled out for the first time his government's apparent intention on the increase granted in January by the board of transport commissioners.

speechtext:
It was very sweet of the Prime Minister to come in and give the debate a bit of focus which it was not getting from the Minister of Transport. He asked us to offer suggestions. One of the first ones we have to offer-and it is not so much a suggestion as

Freight Rates
a conclusion that I would draw-is that in one year you are not going to get a decent royal commission report on a topic of this size unless you instruct the royal commission to go away for six months into retreat and to plow through the information that is available from the previous commission and also from the hearings that have taken place before the board of transport commissioners.
The fundamental problem in our whole railway policy, according to Mr. Currie who has prepared the longest, most detailed and most difficult book on it, is this. He boiled it down. As he said, it could be expressed in one sentence. It was that Canadians had never made up their minds whether they wanted their transportation policy to be socialistic or free enterprise. In other words, we have never made up our minds whether we are going to be for subsidization all the way across the board wherever possible or whether the railways are expected to operate as business units.
It seems to me that if you are going to charge a royal commission with the investigation of the railways there is a real starting point, namely should the royal commission not advise us as to whether the railways are supposed to operate as business organizations or whether they are institutions operating in the public interest and so the question of profit does not enter into it at all. This sort of hybrid arrangement that we have at the present time with the Canadian Pacific Railway supposedly operating as a free enterprise concern and the Canadian National Railways operating as a government concern needs resolving. That is what the royal commission really should do. It certainly cannot do it in one year, and thresh out a policy like this. That is why the whole idea of this being an interim measure and that we are going to get some magic report is rather nonsense. The very number of people who will want to appear before this royal commission when it has hearings I think is an indication that it is going to take more than a year.
The minister said earlier that it took from 15 years to maybe 30 years to begin to appreciate and understand freight rates. I am wondering where we are going to get for this royal commission the personnel with that kind of experience. The only place that I know of where you can get it is from the board of transport commissioners. As they are already constituted, why not let them handle this particular job?
One of the things the hon. member for Laurier mentioned that the commission should investigate fits into this picture of free enterprise or socialism, namely this question of

non-productive lines. You get some really stupid examples. We had one in our region where the C.P.R. ran a railway into Manitou-wadge from the south and the C.N.R. ran one in from the north. There is not enough traffic to keep either one going on a really prosperous basis. This is something that happened recently, within the last three or four years. It is a typical example of mismanagement or poor planning or something like that. However, somebody is stuck with the result and I have a hunch that it is the people of Canada.
I think one of the decisions that really needs to be made very firmly by this royal commission is what is to be done about nonproductive lines. Do we go along with them or do we not? As the minister knows, _ every time there is a suggestion of reduction in service, howls go up. I know that I happen to have more railway division points in my constituency than has anybody else in Canada. I have six of them. Last year when the Canadian National Railways was taking off one of its transcontinental trains a tremendous uproar went up and as a result of the uproar the Canadian National Railways reversed its decision. The decision must have been reversed because it was in the public interest. Here is a typical example of public interest determining something that the president of the C.N.R. had said was uneconomic. Hence essential to this whole problem of the commission in its terms of reference and what it is going to decide is the decision whether we are going to have a national transportation policy based upon the general interest of the country or whether we are going to go on with this half and half system, of pseudo free enterprise and pseudo socialism. I hope that the terms of reference will be such that the royal commission can come up with some real answers.
The hon. member for Laurier mentioned another aspect, as did the hon. member for Vancouver East, namely that the study has to be more than just a study of railway freight rates. The largest pressure groups in this whole field of freight rates or the most vocal and vociferous ones are the ones in relation to trucking. There is also the question of the international aspect of rates and the water rates with the water shippers that need to be studied closely. In other words, from railway freight rates you immediately branch out into all forms of transportation. You cannot consider freight rates without looking at passenger tariffs because they are indivisible in terms of the service that is being provided, since trains have to run over the same rails and the same provisions for one kind of service are used in another. I therefore suggest that the terms

of reference should be extremely broad and that the commission should be encouraged to bring in a complete report setting out a national transportation policy for the government and for the people of Canada, not for five years nor for ten years but for the foreseeable future.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport) moved
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MORTGAGES, CERTIFICATES, PILOTS, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill S-3, to amend the Canada Shipping Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the amendments proposed by this bill are for the most part of a technical nature and many of the clauses represent merely a clarification in wording or a tidying up of existing legislation. Since there will be ample opportunity to discuss these technical details in the committee to which this bill will be referred I will not go into detail on them at the present time. They cover such matters as registration of mortgages on vessels, definition of international voyages and of minor waters, certification of officers and engineers, inspection requirements, and so on. Apart from this the principal clauses in the bill deal with the certain aspects of marine pilotage.
For some years officials of the Department of External Affairs have represented to us that the existing section 346, which provides exemptions from the compulsory payment of pilotage dues, is discriminatory against foreign flag ships in that the exemptions apply only to ships registered in Her Majesty's dominions. Such discrimination is contrary to the provision of a number of treaties in force between Canada and other states, such as the United States, dealing with navigation matters. With the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway and the expected extension of the great lakes trade to the gulf of St. Lawrence this point will assume considerable importance. Our treaty obligations require that we be in a position to accord to the ships of the other nations with whom we have these treaties the same kind of treatment as we give to British ships that may be engaged in the same trade, but the present section 346 does not permit exemption to be granted to any ships but those under the British flag. A proposed amendment will correct this situation.
Perhaps it would be well at this time, Mr. Speaker, for me to say an additional word of explanation concerning this matter of compulsory payment of pilotage dues. There is at present no compulsory pilotage in Canada.	The view	has
been held that the master of a ship must be responsible for the safety of his ship, and the decision must rest with him as to whether or not he requires local assistance in navigating narrow waters. The Canada Shipping Act in section 340 is quite specific on this point.
When a district has been declared by the governor in council to be one in which the

Canada Shipping Act
payment of pilotage dues is compulsory, certain exemptions apply covering naval ships, government ships, fishing vessels and other small vessels, and ships regularly employed in the domestic trade. However, certain of the exemptions made under the provisions of section 346 may be withdrawn by the pilotage authority of the district by bylaw approved by the governor in council.
We also feel that it should be within the power of the pilotage authority, with the approval of the governor in council, to adjust or add to these exemptions according to the changing times. That is, we believe that just as the government has power now to withdraw exemptions power should also exist to add to the exemptions. This would, however, be done only if a master or mate possessed full confidence and experience to navigate in a pilotage district without the help of a pilot. Only the pilotage authority is in a position to reconcile the sometimes apparently conflicting interests of the pilots and their employers who are the masters or owners of the ships they serve.
The other pilotage amendment covered in clause 10 of the bill is a different matter. It provides for a new part VIA under the heading "Great Lakes Pilotage", and I would ask hon. members when considering this part of the bill to separate it completely from the provisions of part VI of the act. There has never been a pilotage district west of Kingston, Ontario on the great lakes. The masters and officers of the regular lake vessels are, of course, familiar with the waters which they ply, and when the occasional ocean vessel entered the great lakes it was the practice for the master to employ a man who, to distinguish him from the licensed pilots in the St. Lawrence, was referred to as a "sailing master". These sailing masters remained on the ocean ships throughout their voyages on the great lakes and assisted the foreign masters through the narrow channels and in the entrances to the ports. The sailing masters took their rest while the ships were on the open waters of the lakes.
It is obvious that whatever arrangement is made for pilotage on the great lakes should be a reciprocal one as between Canada and the United States, and we have held a number of discussions with the United States authorities on this subject. We do not as yet, however, know the exact form of any legislative action they may take in this regard. However, our sections dealing with pilotage on the great lakes are so designated as to permit us to proceed independently, or to fit in virtually with any scheme which the United States authorities may develop, and also provide for reciprocity with the United States in recognition of pilots' licences or

certificates either government may issue. Our basic approach is that within restricted waters which will be defined by the governor in council full pilotage should be required, while elsewhere on the open waters we should at least be satisfied that the ship is carrying a navigating officer or officers fully competent to handle the ship in the open waters.
To summarize the proposed part VIA, it is intended as enabling legislation to empower the governor in council, at a time and to such degree as may be deemed expedient, to require the employment of local pilots by ocean vessels when in the restricted waters of the great lakes; also to take the necessary steps to ensure that every ocean vessel has on board officers who know the rules of the road for the great lakes and can speak English sufficiently to use the radio-telephone.
The only other clause of the bill still to be mentioned is clause 9, which provides that a pilot licensed by the United States authorities for waters forming part of the boundary waters is not committing an offence when he takes his ship across the boundary line. The need for this is obvious when one considers that Canadian pilots must cross and re-cross the boundary line when taking ships up and down the St. Lawrence.
At the conclusion of second reading it is my intention to move that this bill be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for more detailed examination.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MORTGAGES, CERTIFICATES, PILOTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house I am sure will welcome the statement which the hon. minister has made with reference to the second reading of an act to amend the Canada Shipping Act. There are in this bill some sections which are entirely innocuous. There are other sections, on the other hand, which are contentious, and I would like to direct my attention to those sections of the bill which it seems to me are of a very serious nature. I am prompted to say that these sections should not be passed without the most serious consideration. There are several sections that 1 consider contentious and to which I know the house and the committee will want to give the most careful and serious consideration. These sections the hon. minister has already referred to in general, and I shall not deal with them specifically until I come to them.
In the first place, the question that comes to my mind is this. Why is this legislation necessary? The hon. minister in his statement has given no reason why this legislation should be passed at this time. I presume that the bill is brought down because of

the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway, which will take place some time next month. But while that is the pretext I think the main reason for this legislation is the insistence of the United States to enact this measure.
It seems to me that we should not be asked to pass this kind of legislation until we know what the legislation in the United States congress is going to be. Last year there was a bill brought before congress; it did not go through. We know what the nature of that bill is; I have a copy of it here in my file. But the bill which is now before the United States congress, even if it does goes through all of its stages, cannot possibly be passed until October or November of this year. So I ask the question: Are we being asked to pass this kind of legislation before we know what the concurrent legislation on the other side is likely to be? The minister a moment ago used the expression "reciprocal legislation". Well, this is not reciprocal legislation. It is unilateral legislation. It cannot be reciprocal legislation until the two parties have agreed to what they want in the legislation.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MORTGAGES, CERTIFICATES, PILOTS, ETC.
speechtext: And they have not agreed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MORTGAGES, CERTIFICATES, PILOTS, ETC.
speechtext:
And they have not agreed, as the hon. member says. I say respectfully to the minister and to the house that we should not be asked to pass legislation of this kind until an agreement has been reached with our friends on the other side, because we are going to be at a tremendous disadvantage if this legislation is put through unilaterally as I consider it.
Now I come to another question: why is this legislation required? I can see no reason why such legislation as this should be required at this time. It may be necessary in 12 months time; it may be necessary at another date, but it is certainly not necessary now, and the proof of this contention is that there have been any number of ships-deep draft vessels, perhaps not ships drawing 25J feet of water, but certainly ocean trampers- which have been going up to the head of the lakes and passing through the St. Lawrence without the necessity of this kind of legislation. This has been going on now since 1947, and according to the evidence which was given in the other place, one pilot stated there were as many as 744 voyages made, I believe, in 1958. This was done by virtue of the present sections of the Canada Shipping Act, and under the appropriate sections of that act, without regard to the bill which is now before us. There is in the act all the power and all the force necessary to deal with the situation which might arise because of the opening of the
Canada Shipping Act
St. Lawrence seaway. So I ask again: Why should this bill be enacted at the present time.
The next question which comes to my mind is this: Who is asking for this legislation? The St. Lawrence seaway authority does not want it; the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation, which is the United States entity, does not want it; the state department in the United States does not want it; the department of commerce in the United States does not want it. But the United States coastguard wants it. I am almost prepared to go a step further and say that I believe the officials of the Department of Transport deep down in their hearts do not want this legislation either. What has happened is that the coastguard service has put it into their minds that it must have this legislation, and before even it is passed in the congress of the United States they come and ask us to enact a measure of this kind.
I say, with respect to the house, that we should not be asked to pass this sort of legislation because it is not enough to be told- and I say this with respect-by a foreign power that this is necessary. And in effect that is what is happening; the Department of Transport is being pushed around, and the Canadian government is being pushed around at this moment by the demand for the implementation of this bill. We should know why this legislation is required. As it is now, the bill before the congress of the United States provides for certain features which are not acceptable to Canada, and if they are not acceptable to Canada, how do we know that this type of legislation will not affect us in some way or another, and that it may not affect us detrimentally.
How did the minister proceed when he decided, for instance, to implement tolls? There was a section in the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act which clearly said that the St. Lawrence seaway authority could establish tolls either by itself or concurrently with the United States. What hap-ened was that the seaway authority set up a tolls committee jointly with the seaway development corporation. It was the tolls committee which made an agreement, and the minister came to this house and asked the house to approve the agreement which had been made by the two countries. That, I submit, is the way in which the minister should have proceeded in this case and there could be no complaint about that because it would be an agreement made between Canada on the one side and the United States on the other and implemented by parliament.

Canada Shipping Act
Why do we not proceed in the same manner in this instance? After all, pilotage is important. Pilotage is as important as tolls, and tolls are as important as pilotage. Why is there not a committee composed of a group of three Canadians and a group of three Americans to determine questions of pilotage in the international section of the river, that is to say from St. Regis to the head of the lakes? If we had such a committee, and if an agreement were consummated, we could implement it by way of legislation. But there is no agreement. All we know is that there is a bill before congress, and that this bill, as I have said, may have serious implications for us. I submit once again we should not be asked to pass this legislation until we see the United States legislation and know what it is going to be. What harm will be done if we carry on for another year in the same way as we did in 1958 when 744 voyages were made from the great lakes and the St. Lawrence to ports overseas?
There is another point which comes to my mind and it is one which has not been cleared up yet. It is this: is this legislation valid? I have grave doubts about the validity of this legislation. I may be quite wrong, but I know that there are a number of prominent lawyers who share this view, namely that legislation of this kind cannot and should not be implemented by parliament unless based upon agreement, as I said earlier, or upon a treaty. There should be a treaty or an agreement covering pilotage in international waters. This should be brought before the house and the subject of the agreement or treaty should be implemented by legislation. Even if legislation were required, which I doubt and which I deny, then I say that this is not the method we should use-the passing of legislation which the minister has called reciprocal or concurrent but which, really, is unilateral legislation. In my opinion the course of action to be followed is quite clear-and this is what I said earlier-namely that Canada and the United States should come to an agreement on the subject and that it should be implemented by this house.
What is this going to mean with reference to costs? This is an important matter. There was some discussion earlier about the costs which the seaway is going to bring about and, of course, I now speak of costs in the sense of tolls only. Does the house know that if it is considered by some that tolls on the seaway are high the pilotage which is going to be brought about by this legislation is going to be even higher than the costs brought about by tolls on the seaway, so that if there are elements in Canada or elsewhere that think the tolls on the
seaway are high, because of this legislation the costs will be greatly increased.
We must be careful not to play into the hands of the opponents of the St. Lawrence seaway. There have been groups outside of this country that have opposed the St. Lawrence seaway down through the years. When they were finally defeated in the congress of their own country and saw that there was no hope in stopping the seaway they then proceeded to carry on a fight to make the tolls on the seaway so high that they would be prohibitive and make it impossible to move traffic competitively and as well succeed in amortizing the costs of the seaway.
I am afraid that if we pass this legislation without knowing more about its consequences we will be playing into the hands of the opponents of the seaway. These people have but one thing in mind. They have continued by intense lobbying both in the United States and indirectly in this country in favour of high costs for ships moving up and down the St. Lawrence and the great lakes.
I repeat that we do not need this legislation at this time. I suggest instead that there should be a complete overhaul of the Canada Shipping Act with a study of the matters that are dealt with in this legislation. I know what the minister will be prompted to say. He will likely ask, "Why did you not do it when you were on this side of the house?" I will admit at once that perhaps I should have. Possibly I did not realize in the early days when I was on the other side of the house how important this statute was. This is one of the most important statutes to have been passed by this parliament, but it is outmoded and outdated and should be modernized and brought up to date by means of a commission. But over and above modernizing the statute the commission should consider the question of pilotage and the other matters that are under discussion in this legislation. It seems to me that a commission could be very rapidly established. I could suggest names to the minister for that purpose and I know he would consider them very carefully although perhaps not act upon them. Be that as it may, I think there should be a further study of the Canada Shipping Act and of this legislation before we are asked to give these amendments our approval.
There exist now in this act, as I intend to prove, all the sections and powers that the governor in council or the minister need to deal with this situation, to accomplish everything the minister seeks to accomplish without the necessity of this amendment. I

appreciate that that is a far-sweeping statement but I believe I shall be able to establish the validity of it as I go along.
The powers to which I have referred are to be found in many sections of the act but particularly in sections 323 to 329. If the minister will not accede to my request and consider that the time is not yet ripe for this legislation, then I ask him to give consideration to the suggestion that any legislation at this time having to do with the Canada Shipping Act, in the light of what has transpired on the St. Lawrence and the great lakes, should seek to ensure that all advantages be gained by the opening of the seaway. Any legislation at this time should make sure that neither ocean shipping or domestic shipping will be injuriously affected by what is now before the house.
As I said earlier, the legislation arises out of the insistence of the United States authorities to pass a pilotage bill before congress which may well be detrimental to Canadian interests. It appears that the United States authorities and particularly the coastguard want a law that will make pilotage compulsory on the great lakes for ocean vessels other than Canadian or United States vessels by forcing such vessels to carry an additional officer to the normal complement without by proper enabling legislation creating the machinery which would provide the pilotage service required under the bill, a service which where needed, namely in restricted waters, would only be acceptable and satisfactory if it were government controlled and apt to provide the development of a sufficient pool of trained pilots for these restricted areas where pilotage is necessary for the safety of navigation.
What is important, arising out of the development of the St. Lawrence seaway, is the safety of navigation. That is paramount it seems to me and unless we keep that in mind continually we might well get ourselves into serious difficulties. The government should oppose this legislation and by "this

legislation" I mean the legislation that is now before congress. It should oppose the legislation and protect itself under its own laws as they are now in existence by setting up pilotage authorities in these restricted waters. It should try to convince the United States authorities that the Canadian system of pilotage provides a suitable pattern on which the United States government could rely to pass enabling legislation providing for the organization of a similar system in the United States which would permit joint administration of pilotage in the restricted waters of the great lakes.
I come back again to the idea of joint administration and concurrent administration just as there is with reference to tolls. If this were found possible with reference to tolls by means of a committee composed of three Canadians and three Americans, surely the same attitude, the same method and the same procedure could be found possible with reference to pilotage. I have no doubt that if the government pursued it in that light, there could be no difficulty whatsoever. The most serious and flagrant danger of this bill is the one that is contained in clause 8 with which I shall deal on another occasion.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it 10 o'clock?
